items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典小提琴手 Mats Edén 与挪威音乐家 Tellef Kvifte（主奏竖笛及其他乐器）及其子鼓手 Knut Kvifte Nesheim 共同录制，选取两国传统曲调进行重新演绎。三位演奏者均长期探索跨流派融合，小提琴手致力于将不同音乐风格融入瑞典民间音乐，Kvifte 曾是挪威跨界先驱乐队 Slinkombas 的成员，横笛、萨克斯与风笛并用。专辑虽以舞曲素材为主，却更像室内乐——三位乐手沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，挖掘旋律背后隐藏的意义与暗流。开篇选用意象深刻的挪威 Setesdal 山谷小提琴曲《Fossgrimen》，呼应瀑布精灵从水神处学琴、提琴被视为魔鬼乐器的传说。各曲编配细腻，以纹理化伴奏与碎片化结构展开，营造出深沉的氛围与传统之外的可能性。

items.body: EYAA takes its name from a cry of encouragement tied to trance. The French-Ghanaian trio put out “Luku Luku” on Sharma Records on 2 October, the first of five singles leading to their first EP. The voice is Kyekyeku‘s, a singer and guitarist from Accra who now lives in Bayonne, in south-west France, and has worked with highlife veterans Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor. He formed the seven-piece Ah! Kwantou in 2019, and two of its members, bassist Kevin Bucquet and drummer Fred Faure, are the other two thirds of EYAA. In EYAA, Bucquet plays synths and runs the machines as well as the bass, and he, Faure and Kyekyeku composed “Luku Luku” together, with Kyekyeku writing the words. Kyekyeku sings in Twi, pidgin and English over Faure’s drums and Bucquet’s bass, with synths and machines adding the electronics, and the grooves draw on afro-funk, highlife and afrobeat to make an afro-electro built for dancing. This year the trio has played in France, in Accra at Les Francophonies Festival, and in Portugal at Tom de Festa Festival in Tondela. Listen to “Luku Luku” HERE The post Daily Discovery: LUKU LUKU – EYAA appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Entropia' is the debut studio album by Swedish progressive metal act Pain of Salvation, originallyreleased by Avalon in Japan and later reissued by Inside Out, which would become the band's primarylabel for decades to come. Fronted by eccentric multi-instrumentalist Daniel Gildenl�w, the band wasformed in 1984 under the name Reality, gradually evolving into the excellent project we recognizetoday as PoS. As for the album 'Entropia' itself, it had been in the works for quite some time priorto its release. And while most debut albums tend to be uneven and unpredictable, I find thisparticular one to be a surprisingly well-executed amalgamation of styles and influences that allowsthe band's own identity to shine through as well. Primarily a progressive metal album, 'Entropia'seems to draw as much from Faith No More and Mike Patton as it does from bands like Dream Theaterand Fates Warning, with which it shares some similarities. There is a claustrophobic, dark, andalmost urban atmosphere on this record, which to me is in line with what other prog metal acts hadbeen exploring stylistically around that time.The music on 'Entropia' is nevertheless difficult to describe, as it ranges from melodic andstraightforward progressive rock, to chaotic, technical, and rhythmically dynamic heavy prog. Highlyeclectic, this album occasionally feels overstimulating and difficult to follow, which is somethingthe band would remedy on future releases. On top of that, the concept behind 'Entropia' is quitecomplicated, too, and the band does not make it easy to decipher either. So try not to dig too muchinto the lyrics or the meaning behind each track but rather enjoy the dense rollercoaster of stylesand moods that this collection represents. For me 'Entropia' carries several characteristic elementsof the classic Pain of Salvation sound, but they are underdeveloped on this debut LP. Of course,attentive listeners will find plenty of curious elements and motifs scattered throughout the record,and in particular on stronger tracks like '! (Foreword)', 'Winning a War', 'People Passing By', 'Tothe End', and 'Nightmist'. And while this is not a favorite Pain of Salvation album of mine, I mustadmit that as a document of the progressive metal scene of the late 90s it is impressive andpromising.
items._genre: progressive metal / eclectic prog / avant-garde metal
items._cn_summary: Pain of Salvation 1997年首张专辑《Entropia》融合多种风格，在前卫金属框架中融入Faith No More和Mike Patton式的不羁气质，以及Dream Theater和Fates Warning的技术性。整体氛围偏向都市感和都市压抑感，作品在旋律化前卫摇滚与混乱、技术化、节奏多变的重型前卫之间自由切换，偶有过度密集、难以跟随之感。专辑概念复杂且未作清晰阐释，歌词含义晦涩，建议将其视为一场风格与情绪的密集过山车。乐评认为这张首作虽非作者最爱的PoS专辑，但作为乐队声音雏形的雏形与九十年代末前卫金属场景的见证，展现了可期的潜力。推荐曲目包括《! (Foreword)》《Winning a War》《People Passing By》《To the End》与《Nightmist》。

items.body: Review by Andis — Here's a record that deserves a lot more love. We Never Lost Control is one of those albums Igenuinely enjoy, and every spin leaves me in a better mood than before. After all, what's the pointof music if it doesn't entertain you and put a smile on your face?This album will never be mentioned in the same breath as the undisputed giants of progressive rock,but that hardly matters. It's a record I keep coming back to, and one I enjoy tremendously. Germanoddballs Nine Days Wonder, a band that seemed determined to reinvent themselves with every release,followed up their wonderfully bizarre debut by making a complete stylistic U-turn. The result is analbum that's surprisingly difficult to pin down.If I had to try, I'd place it somewhere between David Bowie and Van der Graaf Generator, with atouch of Genesis and Nektar sprinkled on top. What they play could broadly be called progressiverock, but that's only part of the story. There's glam rock swagger, flashes of krautrock, bursts ofhard rock, hints of jazz rock, and all of it fronted by a wonderfully (!) theatrical vocalist. Inother words, this album stubbornly refuses to sit in a single genre box.The band's greatest strength is its energy. Driven by swirling organs and keyboards, backed by aheavy and aggressive bass, they charge through inventive progressive rock that somehow manages tocombine the punch of hard rock with the structure of prog and the occasional hook of melodic pop-rock. Had I not known they were German, I would have guessed they were British without hesitation.Side A is a thoroughly enjoyable affair, filled with melodic songs that contain just enoughprogressive trickery to keep things interesting. But it's on Side B that the real fun begins. Herethe band completely lets loose, delivering colorful, adventurous prog rock with the magnificentnine-minute epic "We Grasp the Naked Meat" as the undisputed centerpiece.We Never Lost Control is a lovable little gem of an album: quirky, energetic, unpretentious, andendlessly entertaining. Think of it as a bag of mixed candy for progressive rock fans. Maybe itisn't a masterpiece, but it's the sort of record that reminds you why digging through the lesser-known corners of the genre can be so rewarding.

items._cn_summary: Nine Days Wonder 的第二张专辑被描述为一次彻底的风格转向，与首作风格截然不同。专辑将前卫摇滚与华丽摇滚的自信、零星闪现的德国泡菜摇滚元素、硬摇滚的爆发力以及爵士摇滚的暗示融合在一起，由一位极具剧场感的歌手统领全碟。编曲由回旋的管风琴与键盘驱动，搭配沉重而具侵略性的贝斯线，在硬摇滚的冲击力与前卫摇滚的复杂性之间取得平衡，同时保留了旋律流行摇滚的钩子。Side A 以富含旋律的曲目为主，夹杂足够的前卫巧思；Side B 则更为放纵，以九分钟史诗《We Grasp the Naked Meat》为核心，将色彩丰富、冒险性的前卫摇滚推向高潮。整体而言，这是一张充满能量、不装腔作势且娱乐性持久的作品，适合作为发掘前卫摇滚边缘地带的入口。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — This is from my blog "Scott's Song by Song Spotlights" with links for listening and purchasing.Clicked 5, but really a 4.5...4 is too low!T.A.P are a progressive rock band led by composer/keyboardist Michael Jobborn. On their first album, which I have not heard (2023's "Paradigms") the band was rounded out by Warr-guitarist/multi-instrumentalist Mark Cook (Phase of Twilight and others) and Guitarist/Vocalist/multi-instrumentalist Suzi James (Fearful Symmetry, whose wonderful latest album "I've Started?So I'll Finish" is reviewed on this blog as well!). Paul Sears and Bill Bachman were both contributors on the first album on the drum throne. This time around Bill Bachman is a full member. Bill is renowned for his work as a drumming educator, including his work with several Drum Corps around the US. (DCI- Drum Corps International- is a deep rabbit hole that I have been familiar with since my college days!) But his prog resume is impressive as well: (From the press release) "Bill is the drummer for Herd of Instinct, Spoke of Shadows, has toured with progressive rock artist Neal Morse, is on recordings with Trey Gunn (King Crimson), Colin Edwin (Porcupine Tree), Adam Holzman (Miles Davis & Steven Wilson), and Gerald Albright (Grammy award winning saxophonist)". So, the musical talent in this band is absolutely staggering!This album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire Rallo of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I receive no additional compensation and am free to "call it like I hear it". In fact, when I received the email offering this review to me from Anne-Claire, I replied, "You had me at Suzi James". The album "Paradigms II" is to be released on October 3, 2026, on the Prog Rock Essentials label (Ordering info follows the review). As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Time to dig into the music!T.A.P are:Michael Jobborn - concepts, keysMark Cook - Warr guitar, bass, 12-string guitar, synth, sitar, strings, choirSuzi James - acoustic/electric guitars, keys, flute, violinBill Bachman - drums, percussionAdditional Contributors on tracks:2. Chris Gill - guitarChris Messina - synth4. Steve Bonino - guitar, lyrics/vocals5. Gayle Ellett - mellotron, acoustic/electric guitars6. Massimo Pieretti - piano, synthGayle Ellett - bouzouki, mellotron8. Tenk van Dool - mandolin, guitarChris Gill - guitarTrack 1 - Galaxy Unknown (4:28)An organ riff, accented with drums starts us off with an odd meter. The rest of the band soon joins in. There is a guitar solo after around 45 seconds. A softer section follows with alternating acoustic and electric instruments in the spotlight. This is a wonderful instrumental musical journey with many layers. As one might expect, the talent level here is through the roof! A terrific opener!Track 2 - A Beacon of Light (12:17)This one fades in with some guitar effects and synth tones. It feels like the first rays of sunlight at dawn, matching the title. Electric piano chords bring a sense of rhythm. The bass line provides melodic movement. The chords are layered among many instruments, giving a rich tonal palate. This is moving at a moderately slow tempo and a relaxed feel. The guitar solo that happens at around the 4-minute mark brings a balance of melodicism and complexity. A droning section after that leads to an upbeat groove on the bass and drums. It begins to take on a jazz fusion flavor. Synth and guitar solos float over the top of the rhythm bed. Just before 7:30 things calm down and a new section begins. Sitar sounds are a part of the soundscape. Bill's marching band experience shows in his snare part. At 8:45 we are down to lead guitar, bass and keys. The drums subtly return. We are in a slower 6-8 at this point. At 9:55 a more strident beat that reminds me of old TV themes takes over. There are so many moods in this piece; I love it! At 11:30, it reminds me of how it began. What an absolutely fantastic instrumental piece of music!Track 3 - A Dramatic Interlude (4:06)Electric piano, bass and lead guitar start this off. The drums enter a moment later. This is in a moderately slow 6-8, so far, but the title tells me something is going to happen. The tempo increases slightly and becomes more rhythmic after a small crescendo. I believe that is the Warr guitar taking the solo that follows. I love the staccato bass and guitar riff at around 2:20. Things begin to build up at around 3:20. The track ends with a long, sustained chord. A wonderful piece, but not as dramatic as the title indicated. Track 4 - A Hole in the Ground (6:14)Rich electric piano chords and clean guitars start us off here. Lead guitar emerges. And then--Vocals! Guest musician Steve Bonino is on this track with guitars and vocals. (This is not the first time his name has appeared in one of my reviews!) The drums begin to emerge as we progress. Mark Cook's basslines are fantastic on this album. Steve's voice seems a little buried in the mix at times. The drums might be a little too far back at times, as well. I like the song, but I don't feel like it's mixed as well as it could be. It would benefit from a better presentation. It ends with droning sounds.Track 5 - 4th Dimensional Wave (11:50)Sound effects fade in and guitars join. This starts out sounding like some sort of alarm. Soon, though, the music gets melodic with a fantastic guitar solo; I believe it is Suzi James. We are in a moderately slow tempo. The keys are playing a mellotron style chorus behind the solo. Some intricate rhythmic patterns follow. This keeps building, slowly and gradually. At around 4:20 we get into odd meters. At 5:45, the rhythm shifts into a different groove. I am really enjoying this one! There are tons of changes! Gayle Ellet of Djam Karet and his band the Electromags adds his keyboard abilities to the soundscapes. Probably my favorite track, so far.Track 6 - Lyrical Paradox (3:50)This one has a bit of a swing to it. Sort of a mellow melodic tune. The sound gets bigger just after the one-minute mark. Great melodies in this one. I love the slide guitar in it; it reminds me of the slide guitar in "And You and I" from Yes. This is a nice little piece. Ellet is back with bouzouki on this, and Massimo Pieretti (whom I have reviewed as well) adds keyboards.Track 7 - Outlooks of the Closed-Minded (6:29)This opens with some accents and jazz chords. It has a fusion feel to my ears. I love the syncopated rhythms. It reminds me of the Dixie Dregs a bit. Lots of melodies wind their way through this one. Wonderful track!Track 8 - Wishful Solitude (:)This one is more up-tempo, yet lighthearted. As with most of the album, the melodies are abundant! At around 3:15 Suzi plays her flute. There are many interesting things in the soundscape. At just be for the 5-minute mark, a descending synth part that sounds like the 70s idea of a UFO landing takes over, then we get a bit funky! At around 6:45 we get a psychedelic organ sound. This is a very cool piece with many different things going on. Tenk van Dool (who I am not familiar with) plays the mandolin at around 8:45. The melodies intertwine as we approach the ending. This is a wonderfully arranged prog instrumental. Great way to end this wonderful album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I really liked that a lot! Unfortunately, I am not sure what happened on track 4, "A Hole in the Ground". I have always liked Steve Bonino's contributions, and he always seems to be a good guy in the online interactions I have had with him, but something just didn't work for me on that track. Otherwise, this is a fantastic album of mainly instrumental prog with some fusion tendencies. I give this a 4.5 out of 5 or 90%. Recommended!

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由键盘手Michael Jobborn领衔，结合Warr吉他、原声与电吉他、长笛、小提琴等多种乐器，加上多位客座乐手参与不同曲目，展现出层次丰富的器乐编排。从乐评描述来看，作品以器乐叙事为主，包含管风琴开场、合成器音色的渐进铺垫、不同段落间音色与配器的交替切换，以及融入西塔琴、布祖基琴、曼陀林等世界音乐元素。Bill Bachman担任鼓手，为整体节奏结构增添了稳固支撑。乐评者认为乐队演奏水平极高，作品在变拍与段落衔接上展现出一定复杂性。作为折衷主义前卫摇滚作品，它在器乐融合与跨文化音色方面有一定尝试，但整体仍以传统前卫摇滚框架为主，对追求更极端实验或即兴自由方向的听众而言可能显得保守。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — First it was FAIRPORT CONVENTION, but STEELEYE SPAN really planted the flag, and so were followed by worthy extenders in other lands, such as MALICORNE and TRI YANN in France, ANGELO BRANDUARDI and GIAN CASTELLO in Italy, CLANNAD and HORSLIPS in Ireland, MABSANT and PERERIN in Wales, CAPERCAILLIE and RUNRIG in Scotland, OUGENWEIDE and GALAHAD in Germany, MILLADOIRO and SANGRE DE MUERDAGO in Spain, and on and on. Most played a mix of trad/arranged and original/arranged trad style, such that, if you didn't already know, you'd be challenged to distinguish one from the other. They translated ancient poetry and prose into their native language and took liberties with the original melodies when they were known at all. I count myself among those who didn't realize that at least one Finnish group belongs in such select company, but given the breadth of Finnish prog folk, which is like THIS wide, I can't say I'm surprised by the presence or the quality of TARUJEN SAARI ("the island of sagas"), right from this debut.Led by the spirited and technically irreproachable vocals and woodwinds of Kaisa Saari, the hurdy gurdy and sundry from veteran TAPIO MATTLAR, twin violins, and a host of other folk instrumentation, this opening shot straddles all the aforementioned genealogical lines and draws a few of their own. When they choose a tune already well known to the type of people who would listen to this album in the first place, like "The Blacksmith", they give it a fresh spin, in this case it's more potent than the diva-ish LOREENA MCKENNITT rendition or the dirge like versions by STEELEYE SPAN when they were still finding themselves. They even tap the Swedes for the insistent "Margareeta". But the obvious standout here is Sinun Siniset silmasi" (your blue eyes), which merges flawless vocals, organic melody and guest cello.It's worth mentioning that for 30+ years a world beat group named VAARTINA has decorated their own room in trad oriented Finnish folk to an appreciative audience, but TARUJEN SAARI in unison pushes against the 4 (or however many) walls and thus, if not on the island of which they sing, can at least see it from their terrasse.
items._genre: folk / progressive folk / nordic folk
items._cn_summary: 这张芬兰前卫民谣专辑以丰富的传统乐器配置——手摇风琴、双小提琴、木管乐器以及人声为核心，展现了北欧民谣的独特气质。乐评将之置于欧洲各国传统民谣复兴运动的谱系中，与Fairport Convention、Steeleye Span等经典团体的传承脉络相并列。乐队对经典曲目如《The Blacksmith》进行了重新诠释，超越了Loreena McKennitt及Steeleye Span早期较为戏剧化或哀歌式的处理方式，呈现出更具活力的版本。专辑还改编了瑞典民谣《Margareeta》，并融入客座大提琴演奏。作品以芬兰语演唱本土改编的古老诗歌与散文，原创与改编之间的界限模糊。这种对北欧传统民谣的深度挖掘与跨界融合，对于关注世界音乐与前卫民谣交叉领域的听众具有参考价值。

items.body: Review by bandtutu — Drowning Steps - The Bravery of a Tireless Mind: Book One1. The Angels and the PlaygroundThe Angels and the Playground is an excellent introduction to the album. I really like the way it begins to develop the character's story. One detail I particularly love is the sound of the pencil writing on paper. It may seem like something simple, but it really adds to the immersion in the narrative. Caio's vocals also deserve praise, as they fit the song's concept very well and help convey the emotions behind the story.The first three minutes are beautiful. The acoustic guitar is very well crafted, and the atmosphere at the beginning reminds me of moments from "The Moon Touches Your Shoulder" by Porcupine Tree and "A Pillow of Winds" by Pink Floyd. There is a nostalgic tranquility to this introduction that I really enjoy, with a delicate arrangement that allows each element to find its own space. The song progresses naturally, without rushing, and never becomes tedious.Around 4:15, we get an incredible transition. The guitar riff, accompanied by the keyboards and synthesizers, changes the whole dimension of the composition and creates one of the first major moments of the song. I really like how these elements complement each other. The acoustic guitar picking that comes in here, breaking up the rhythm, also deserves praise.At 6:30, the distorted guitar introduces a section that, although I understand its importance to the narrative and the character's emotional context, buy simply doesn't work for me. I really don't like the riff. I understand the intention behind the change and recognize its purpose within the song, but I feel another approach could have conveyed the same feeling in a better way. It's a very personal criticism, especially because the composition wins me back shortly afterward.At 7:37, another guitar riff comes in, accompanied by the synthesizer, and the result is excellent. The drums also deserve praise, as the changes in the groove give the composition more personality. I really like the bass's rich and distinctive tone, and for me, this combination works so well that it makes up for much of what bothered me in the previous section.At 9:07, after a very striking, almost ghostly break, the song moves into a section that reminds me of "Moonloop" by Porcupine Tree. Even though this is a relatively long passage, it never becomes tedious. The instrumental development keeps me interested and shows the band's ability to sustain extended sections without simply relying on the repetition of the same idea.At 10:47, a riff with a more metal feel begins to emerge. I can't quite define exactly what kind of sound it is, but I really like the change. It's the kind of riff I would even like to write myself, both because of its sound and the energy it carries. Just a few seconds later, at 11:02, another transition completely changes the emotional state of the song. The arrangement takes on a different dimension, setting the stage for one of my favorite moments of the track.The keyboards entering at 11:23 are simply incredible. The piano comes in with a very emotional quality, adding a special sensitivity to everything that had been building up until that point. This section really moved me, especially because of the way the instrument transforms the atmosphere without needing an exaggerated change in intensity. Thiago's work on the keyboards is fundamental here, showing how important his contributions are to the musical identity of both the song and the album.When everything seems to be heading toward a satisfying conclusion, the guitar comes back and creates a sudden shock that, interestingly enough, works very well for me. I don't see this choice as a problem, in fact, I really like the effect it creates.However, my biggest criticism comes right after that, at 12:27, when the previously used riff returns. I feel that bringing it back is unnecessary and slightly hurts the flow of the composition. In my opinion, the song had already found an interesting path toward its conclusion, and I didn't like going back to that idea.Still, I really like the grandiose effect created by the keyboards together with the vocals during the "Then we went up, then we went down" section. The combination has a lot of strength and fits the scale of the narrative, although the repetition of this passage became a little boring for me. The ending of the section, with the guitar delay, works well and sets the stage for the final part of the song.The final section is beautiful. After so many changes in intensity and instrumental passages, the song finally reaches a sense of peace that almost feels like a release. The atmosphere reminds me a lot of "Insurgentes" by Steven Wilson. It also gives me the same feeling of relief I get when "Raider II" ends and "Like Dust I Have Cleared from My Eye" begins on Grace for Drowning. After such a long emotional journey, it feels like you can finally breathe.Despite some choices that don't completely work for me, "The Angels and the Playground" is a very strong opening, with excellent instrumental moments, engaging dynamic shifts, and an atmosphere that contributes just as much to the musical experience as it does to the narrative.------------------------------------2. Fragments of a LifetimeI found this song quite interesting, especially because it takes a very different approach from the previous track. It has this kind of progressive folk-ballad feel, with a very atmospheric arrangement. The keyboard effects also remind me a lot of "Entangled" by Genesis, and I think they fit the song really well.I also really liked the ending, when the song starts to give you the feeling that something is going wrong. It's an interesting choice because it works as a lead-in to the next track, "The Nod", leaving a certain sense of tension in the air.I like the idea behind the lyrics, especially this moment where the character is searching for peace. Overall, it's a simple track, but it works really well within the story of the album. --------------------------3. The NodThe beginning of this song reminds me a lot of Opeth atmosphere. Then a very distinctive guitar riff comes in. I wouldn't necessarily say it's good or bad, but I understand the idea behind it and I think it works.I really like the part around 2:35, when a sequenced drum pattern starts playing in the background. I thought that was a very interesting choice, and it reminds me of some things Wilson has done. The drums also deserve some praise here; they give the song a lot of dynamics and help build that sense of tension without simply making everything heavy all the time.The bass solo is also really good, especially with the character's narration playing in the background. Then the heavy guitar riff from the beginning comes back, and this time I think it really gains more meaning and fits the song very well.I also really liked the synthesizer solo, which brings a different texture to the track. The guitar solo is good as well and works nicely within the composition.Overall, I think the song takes its time to show this depth and develop the idea further.----------------------------------------------4. Waiting for RedemptionThis is easily my favorite song on the album. It starts with a piano in the background and Caio's vocals, which once again deserve a lot of praise. I really like how the song gradually builds along with the lyrics, creating more and more tension as it progresses.The way the song keeps building gives me a strong Neal Morse vibe. I can't really say whether it reminds me more of Transatlantic, Spock's Beard, or his solo work, but there is definitely something about the way the song develops that makes me think of those bands.Around 3:50, a guitar riff comes in and fits the song really well. The effects also deserve a lot of praise here. They manage to create a completely different atmosphere and then return to the previous one in a very natural way, without making the transitions feel forced.This particular riff really reminds me of a riff from the bridge of "Weenie Beenie," from Foo Fighters first album. It's not exactly the same, of course, but the way the riff comes in gives me a very similar feeling.Then, around 5:15, the song goes through a complete change. Once again, it shifts into a darkness and more introspective atmosphere.Shortly after that, the synthesizer solo comes in, and together with the drums, it sounds incredible. Listening to it gives me a really good feeling, almost as if I'm going on a trip. And maybe that's exactly what the character is experiencing in the story as well.Then that heavy riff comes back, this time accompanied by a wah-wah guitar solo, and I absolutely love it. It's really spectacular. The combination of the riff, the guitar tone, and the wah-wah works incredibly well.A new verse then comes in, very well placed, followed by the return of that almost ghostly section, which keeps repeating.My only real criticism is that this final part starts to feel a repetitive. I like the atmosphere it creates, but I think it goes on a little longer than it should.Even so, this is easily the track that stands out the most to me. It has so many great ideas that fit together really well, and the way it moves between different atmospheres while maintaining the narrative is excellent.----------------------------5. Life Handed Me the MapThis is the song that closes the album. It feels like the character is expressing his gratitude for having finally found the path; the "map", that will allow him to reconnect with the fragments of his past.I really like the effects and the atmosphere of the song. There is something very calm and reflective about it, which makes it feel appropriate as the ending of the story.I also really like the detail of hearing him write again at the end of the song, followed by the sound of the book closing. I think it's a great way to bring the album to an end, especially because the sound of the pencil writing appeared earlier in the story. It gives the whole thing a feeling of closure, almost as if we've just finished reading the character's story ourselves.--------------Overall Opinion on the AlbumFor me, this is a work that shows how much the band has matured, both in their songwriting and in the way they tell their story. I really enjoyed the songs, especially the way the album manages to create different atmospheres and make them work within the narrative.The main highlights for me were The Angels and the Playground, The Nod, and especially Waiting for Redemption. Overall, this is an album that really surprised me and shows how much Drowning Steps has evolved. It's a record I definitely plan to listen to over and over again, because I feel like there are still a lot of details to discover.-----------My Ratings:4,3/5 8,6/10Congratulations for this excellent work.Caio Claro / vocals, acoustic guitar (1), guitars (2,5), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationFabricio Mendon�a / drumsLeonardo Gon�alves / bassMarcos Duran / guitars (1-4)Tiago Pierucci / keyboards, synthesizers, effects, organ, piano, Wah-Wah guitar (2), backing vocals (4), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationRobin Peachey / vocals (1)La�s Gonzalez / vocals (2)Erlend Viken / vocals (3)

items.body: Turn it off, this channel’s boring, see? This is not how my life was supposed to be So I take this poison inside of me There is a delicious stupidity in trying to escape a miserable situation by making choices almost guaranteed to leave you worse off. The promise of feeling alive again has filled bars, emptied bank accounts, inspired regrettable phone calls, and sent countless people back into relationships they had good reason to leave. New England darkwave outfit Ghost Painted Sky have built Kissing Lions around one of humanity’s more dependable talents: recognizing the jaws directly in front of us and deciding, against every scrap of available evidence, to lean closer anyway. Taken from the forthcoming Failure Blooms, the song captures those moments when boredom and disappointment have accumulated enough weight that almost any escape starts to look reasonable, including the varieties with sharp teeth. The band began in Massachusetts in 2014 as David Strong’s project, expanding into a genuine partnership when vocalist and lyricist Lisa Wood joined in 2018. Guitarist Michael Boudreau followed in 2022, while longtime collaborator Aurora Grabill adds violin here and elsewhere on the album. What they produce on “Kissing Lions” belongs comfortably within darkwave and post-punk, though its real engine is psychological: the familiar urge to make some reckless little bargain with yourself because ordinary life has become intolerably beige. Wood sings from inside that bargain. The rising tide gets pushed away, the television gets switched off, poison gets swallowed, and eventually the lion receives a kiss directly on the mouth. You can practically hear the terrible idea becoming attractive in real time. The metaphor works because lions remain perfectly innocent in this arrangement. They were always going to bite. The speaker is the one grabbing the teeth. “Kissing Lions describes those mostly vain attempts to seize on anything that creates a fleeting feeling of being alive for a moment amid relentless waves of the humdrum, doldrums, and failure, which so often end up being misguided and ultimately just creating a thicker mire even more strangling than the original situation one sought to escape… bad decisions that bite back and create further downward spirals,” says Strong. Strong’s accompanying video stretches that idea across generations, combining 8mm footage shot by his grandfather, Herbert Virta, with material from a 2023 virtual performance for Goths for Sanctuaries and footage from The Heavy Culture Cooperative in Easthampton, Massachusetts, filmed in August 2026 with projected visuals by Daisy. Past and present collide without becoming sentimental window dressing; time simply keeps advancing while people continue finding increasingly elaborate ways to get bitten. Watch the video for Kissing Lions below: The digital maxi-single adds the brighter Kissing Lions (Effervescent Remix) and My Words Are Not My Own, which turns toward conformity and the slow surrender of individual voice. Mixed and mastered by William Faith, Failure Blooms follows 2018’s Flightless. Eight years later, Ghost Painted Sky sounds preoccupied with failure less as an ending than as a remarkably fertile place to keep making the same disastrous choices. Listen to Kissing Lions below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: Ghost Painted Sky 是一支来自美国新英格兰地区的暗潮后朋克三人乐队，2014年由 David Strong 在马萨诸塞州创立，2018年 vocalist Lisa Wood 加入后逐渐成型。专辑《Failure Blooms》中的这首《Kissing Lions》聚焦于人性中明知山有虎偏向虎山行的冲动——在厌倦与失望的重压下，人们往往选择那些几乎注定让处境更糟的逃离路径。歌词以第一人称视角呈现这种自我毁灭式的交易：关掉电视、吞下毒药、亲吻狮口，而狮子本身始终无辜，咬人的决定完全来自主动凑上去的叙述者。歌曲在暗潮与后朋克的框架内运作，核心驱动力来自心理层面的叙事张力而非声响创新。MV 跨越世代，将 Strong 祖父 Herbert Virta 拍摄的 8mm 影像、2023年虚拟演出片段以及 2026年8月在 Easthampton 拍摄的真实现场素材交织在一起，时间在画面中持续推进，人物则不断寻找更精巧的方式去被咬伤。数字 maxi-single 还收录了更明亮的 Effervescent Remix 以及转向探讨从众主题的《My Words Are Not My Own》。

items.body: I had hoped to be seen by you Unbroken gaze like a sweet arrow Could you ever feel my eyes on you Bathing you in my desire Desire has a way of making the body speak before the mind has decided what to say: flushed cheeks, an aching chest, the unreasonable hope that somebody might feel a glance from across the room. In the video for Sacred Hearts, Gloria de Oliveira takes those private sensations onto the streets of Hamburg’s St. Pauli district, where barroom lamps, photo-booth portraits, and the company of women give longing somewhere to live. The song’s burning heart finds a fitting companion in the red lights overhead, while affection passes between its subjects through looks, laughter, and the small pleasure of being together. The Berlin-based German-Brazilian musician and visual artist shares the video for the third single from her forthcoming album The Lying Swans, due October 30, 2026, through La Double Vie and Cargo Records. Produced by Randall Dunn, whose work includes records with Anna von Hausswolff and Marissa Nadler, Sacred Hearts considers the exhilaration and anxiety of giving yourself over to another person, particularly when the body seems to have made that decision ahead of you. The opening guitar figures carry an almost medieval character, joined by bright, percussive tones with the delicacy of a hammered dulcimer. Matt Chamberlain’s drumming briefly suggests the forward motion of Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill before settling into the song’s own gait. Deep resonant strings lend the arrangement weight, while synthesizers soften its edges and extend its peculiar, old-world atmosphere. The tones and melody evoke a folk ballad like Nick Cave’s The Weeping Song, with the spaciousness of a Western just beyond the song’s antique ornamentation. De Oliveira sings into that space with a delicate quiver that evokes Elizabeth Fraser, with a classical poise softened by the intimacy of her delivery. Lennard Zander’s acoustic, electric, and 12-string guitars trace fine melodic lines without disturbing the vocal’s tenderness; Arjan Miranda anchors the arrangement on bass, while de Oliveira, Dunn, and Úlfur Hansson add layers of synthesizer. The music leaves her exposed yet almost weightless, as if every declaration of love might tip her toward losing her footing. The lyrics measure desire through its physical symptoms, moving from fever and sleeplessness toward the hope contained in a hand’s touch. To be seen becomes as urgent as to be loved, and the repeated attempts to contain that feeling only reveal its scale. Yet, the song’s title draws on an image de Oliveira has carried since childhood, joining religious devotion to the unruly sensations of romantic attachment. “The Catholic image of Christ’s Sacred Heart – a heart literally engulfed in flames – has struck me since childhood.” “Of course it’s meant to symbolise God’s boundless and passionate love for mankind – however, as John Keats once wrote, ‘I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the heart’s affections, and the truth of imagination’. And how does it feel to give yourself over to that affection and desire despite fear? With this song, I wanted to capture these seemingly contrasting sentiments.” Shot and directed by award-winning Turkish filmmaker Seda Kaçak, and edited by de Oliveira, the video stars London actress Mona Najma alongside Eva Rogalla. Kaçak follows the women through St. Pauli in handheld close-ups, catching them sharing drinks, posing for photo-booth pictures, and moving between daylight streets and richly coloured interiors. Superimposed faces and starbursts around the lights give these ordinary pleasures an enchanted quality. Conceived as a homage to the bond between women, the film offers an affectionate counterpoint to the song’s solitary ache: companionship makes room for feelings that can otherwise become overwhelming. Watch the video for Sacred Hearts below: A classically trained singer whose acting work includes Babylon Berlin and Christian Petzold’s Undine, de Oliveira released music with the darkwave and synthpop duo lovespells before her 2020 debut album Fascination. Her 2022 collaboration with David Lynch’s longtime sound designer Dean Hurley, Oceans of Time, followed through Sacred Bones. Across those releases, she has explored dream pop, ethereal wave, ambient music, and the influence of her Brazilian roots, alongside work for theatre, film, and London Fashion Week. Recorded in Iceland, New York, and Berlin, The Lying Swans extends those interests across nine songs concerned with trauma, perception, and the difficult return of trust. Its title invokes the myth of Leda, while its literary references include John Keats, Emily Brontë, Anne Sexton, and Milton’s Paradise Lost. Within that broader examination of love and illusion, Sacred Hearts holds open the possibility of affection despite fear. Listen to Sacred Hearts below or via streaming services, and pre-order The Lying Swans here. The album is out October 30, 2026, on digital, vinyl, CD, and cassette. items.body: “Nothing lasts, you see, not even the thoughts inside you. And you musn’t waste your time looking for them. Once a thing is gone, that is the end of it.” – Paul Auster, ‘In The Country of Last Things’. Taking inspiration from ‘In The Country of Last Things’, a 1987 novel written by Paul Auster, ‘Last Things’ seeks to isolate itself in the countryside, distancing itself from the fast pace of the urban lifestyle for something more contemplative and lonely; looking for the literal wilderness after dissatisfaction or unrest. Nature is beautiful and beneficial to one’s health and wellbeing, but it can also be vicious and unpredictable. The countryside can be relaxing and peaceful, but it can also catch someone unawares and leave them reeling, as audiences found out in The Blair Witch Project. A foreboding presence sticks to the prospect of isolation like glue; the stark, swaying branches and the yawning fields can sprout the genre of folk horror with ease, and seemingly without any additional help; it comes from their own design. This complete edition of Last Things takes up three discs and includes music recorded under his The Inventors of Aircraft moniker, further planting Phil Tomsett’s music in the soil. Described as a ‘personal struggle through hum, thunder, and dread’, Last Things is something of an audio artefact, a recently unearthed relic which, when played back, translates Auster’s prose into an earthy type of music. Last Things has lain dormant, entrenched in the damp soil, for time immemorial, long enough to ingratiate itself with the song of the land and the rustling of the fields, only slightly decaying as it ages. Contentedness and a flowering of peace may be held in one hand, but the woods can also be wild, its cabins holding a wolf in disguise of a sweet grandmother. Last Things moves from bejewelled beauty to monumental dread. In some ways, the music is like the exploration of an old house, deep in the country, where spiders have nestled and settled, and the floorboards creak with age, having not had a foot to press upon and upset its wood. Like a self-made contagion, loneliness seeps into the air, mingling with the gathering dreamcatchers of dust. Tracks such as ‘I Long For Days That Never Existed’ and ‘These Are The Last Things, She Wrote’ are indicative of the music having been through rough patches, and its moss-streaked textures seem to creep around the rooms with downcast body language, close to mourning with its lowered head as it looks to retreat back into its shell, locking and bolting the door to this great old house and never leaving, even as the growing vines slink over the windowsills and the day turns to dusk. www.wistrec.com
items._genre: ambient / experimental / drone / dark folk / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这张三碟装专辑受保罗·奥斯特1987年小说《在最后国度的尽头》启发，试图以声音构建远离都市节奏的乡野意象。乐评将其描述为"嗡嗡声、雷鸣与恐惧的个人挣扎"，音乐像一段被深埋泥土的古老遗物，长期休眠后重新出土，将奥斯特的文字转译为带有泥土气息的声响。作品在装饰性美感与巨大恐惧之间游走，铺展蛛网尘埃般的孤独意象，苔藓覆盖的质感渗透于房间角落，低垂的姿态近乎哀悼。曲名如《我渴望从未存在的日子》与《这些是最后的物件，她写道》暗示音乐经历过某种粗糙的磨损，整体呈现介于暗潮氛围、田野录音与低调嗡鸣之间的实验性散文气质，偏向小众独立厂牌发行。

items.body: Can we really imagine death from a love? It’s one of those rare things that happens all too often, painted into the fabric of cotton goods promises and soft-hearted tenderness. Say a love leaves us unexpectedly, dies suddenly, and we are insatiable to that love originally – that could be marked as death from a love. Like something inside us has died, ready to be replaced with something else that we don’t really want to replace at all costs. This is the “love” element, closeness, some would say clinging, but I don’t know about you, love never comes through death… And I don’t know either, whether you also feel how mental transmogrification turns the concept of “it” inside out, with fake society, conceited people, counterfeit claims and all that negative mind-melting stuff that comes through death. Do some people enjoy perverting the concept of death? Of over-dramatising what life is actually always eternal? Seriousness is seriousness, and words are just that – dust in deserts of sound. It is only when we find material serious and mature enough to tranquilise the sheer grief that non-psycopathic people feel that we find albums like “Death From A Love”. It’s a great title, a great album and a great package. One that will last for all eternity in the eyes of those willing to use that oh-so important word: care. You need patience, in other words, to tackle a concept like “Death From A Love”. The weak-minded fall down and have no patience. The creator of this recording has a lot of patience, I would wager. How else could one commit to things that are seen as trite in the minds of the unminded robot-hybrids of our generation? Pedalling out the unreal at every turn – this album is real. From the opening lines, where morose tones touch the back of the neck in a FareWell Poetry style, the anger that we all feel is self-contained and instead of being left to fester, is expressed in musical, and here, reviewer language. It’s the least trade-off a true artist could expect of intelligent life, after all. As represented by electronic skeletons throughout the central coda. In life, nobody is better than anyone else. We are all winners. And every album is a treasure, whether you choose to “like” it or not? And what is like? We may as well be all self-defeatist – I’ll tell you what; we may as well all be Franz Kafka. Never finishing our stories properly – I’ve wrote a lot of those stories over the years. But the deciding factor on whether we keep art in our collections (we are ultimately nerdy collectors if we are perusing this area of music by nature, after all) is if the central concept is a successfully realised one. Come tune in to “Death From A Love” and find out why we have something special. www.homeassemblymusic.bandcamp.com
items._genre: experimental / electronic / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以"死于爱"为核心概念，试图探讨爱与死亡之间的精神变形关系。乐评指出作品开场呈现出阴郁的基调，音色触及后颈般低回，类似FareWell Poetry的处理方式。创作者展现出不急于宣泄的耐心，将愤怒内化为音乐语言，以电子骨架贯穿中段编码段落。专辑整体强调真实性，抵制当代社会中虚假的戏剧化倾向，呼唤对概念本身的深度关注。乐评认为这是一位有耐心的创作者对严肃主题的成熟表达，适合愿意投入时间理解概念的听众。专辑通过音乐化处理普遍存在的悲痛感，在概念完整性与艺术真诚度之间寻求平衡。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了比利时十三支创新乐团的作品，录制于1129年建立的鲁汶郊外帕克修道院。专辑以器乐为主，融合比利时民间与世界音乐传统，涵盖罗姆音阶、bal-musette手风琴风味、地中海与阿拉伯音乐等多重元素。斯洛文尼亚裔小提琴家Rénélius Bikar的泛欧罗姆历史叙事、Django风格的吉普赛摇摆、鲁特琴与阿拉伯语演唱、接近巴洛克的手风琴与羽管键琴组合，以及单簧管独奏与喉音演唱的古老凯尔特联想，呈现出丰富的声音景观。整体在多元风格中保持统一，受修道院建筑与石质自然混响启发，三年制作完成，录音温暖而沉稳。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这是圣多美和普林西比70-80年代音乐的合辑续篇，聚焦当地Puxa音乐这一鲜为人知的非洲流派。Puxa融合了merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种节奏元素，葡萄牙殖民历史和跨大西洋地理位置使其吸收了加勒比海音乐的影响。专辑收录15首作品，展示多把吉他交织缠绕的演奏方式，主唱与和声相互呼应构成旋律框架，贝斯与键盘退场时鼓与吉他主导节奏，形成令人舞动的律动。文章特别指出Puxa舞蹈曾被葡萄牙殖民者禁止但未能成功根除，暗示其与精神召唤或驱魔仪式的关联。整体记录了一个仅有12个村庄、缺乏专业录音设施的小岛国音乐场景，是非洲后殖民时代音乐生态的重要文献。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自丹麦三人组的数字EP处女作，由北欧民谣圈资深主唱Mia Guldhammer领衔。五首曲目大多取材自传统素材，由三位乐手各自注入个人理解。开场曲以粗犷的小跑节奏展示了主唱极具说服力的嗓音；唯一的原创曲目由乐队成员Morten Musicus创作，加入口簧和风笛带来推进感。钦巴龙琴为传统曲目铺设细腻底色，口簧与长笛、弦乐交织的终曲器乐部分则呈现出某种不安分且令人兴奋的质感。整体弥漫着古老、嘎吱作响的氛围，乐队虽初登场却展现出成熟与精湛。然而评论中并未明确展示强烈的实验性或跨界先锋倾向，更偏向传统北欧民谣框架内的精致打磨。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / documentary / sound art
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑并非传统意义上的音乐作品，而是声音记录者伊恩·布伦南在芝加哥南区枪支暴力幸存者聚集的街头所采集的现场录音素材。25位参与者年龄从17岁到67岁不等，许多人刚刚参加或即将参加悼念仪式，暴力创伤几乎覆盖了社区中的每一个人。录音在一栋94岁长辈住宅的前廊完成，正值特朗普下令向该市部署国民警卫队的当天。除了少数即兴说唱之外，内容基本是口述证词：有老人失去两个儿子后反复道歉，有年轻人主动讲述自己的经历。编辑选择直接呈现录音者本人简短的解说与原始声音材料，强调不加任何音乐添加的原则。项目收益捐赠给以公共卫生方法遏制暴力的国际组织，整体更像一份田野录音文献与声音艺术作品。

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — The third album of my beloved Procol Harum, "A salty dog". The last one with Dave Knights on bass guitar and the last one as well with Matthew Fisher on keys, who he also did the production on this one. Now, "A salty dog", is a much more laid-back record than the two previous of the band, yet is so so beautiful. Mostly blues-based with a progressive direction, and always having the distinctive Procol Harum sound, meaning piano and voice driven. When Gary Brooker first performed the piece "A salty dog" on piano, the room was filled with sunlight shining through the windows. The drummer, B.J. Wilson, with a sunbeam on his face, told Brooker he thought it was the most beautiful song he had ever heard. Gary Brooker delivers some vein-cutting vocals throughout the album. Matthew Fisher did the lead vocals on three tracks on this one, "Boredom", "Wreck of the Hesperus" and "Pilgrim's progress". The track "Crucifiction" is a lament with ripping lead vocals provided by Robin Trower. A really beautiful album, closing a chapter for Procol Harum.
items._genre: crossover prog / blues rock / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 这是Procol Harum第三张专辑，也是贝斯手Dave Knights和键盘手Matthew Fisher参与的最后一张作品。专辑延续了乐队标志性的钢琴与人声主导风格，以布鲁斯为根基融入前卫摇滚方向，氛围比前两张更为放松内敛。Gary Brooker的演唱贯穿始终，嗓音极具穿透力，Fisher在三首曲目中担任主唱，Robin Trower则在《Crucifiction》中献上撕裂感十足的演唱。标题曲在创作时即被鼓手B.J. Wilson形容为听过的最美旋律。整体而言，这是一张以传统摇滚乐器配置为载体的渐进式作品，在编曲和声音设计上偏向经典摇滚的抒情路线，融合了一定的布鲁斯即兴元素，结构上具备一定的渐进式发展，但整体仍处于主流摇滚的审美范畴内，与用户偏好的实验、爵士、电子、暗潮等方向距离较远。
